query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Switching from a full-melt, laser‐based additive manufacturing process to a binder jetting/ink‐extrusion process followed by isothermal sintering will reduce thermal gradients, limit segregation and residual stress and thereby improve the mechanical integrity of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi alloy powder produced via mechanical alloying, which has a tendency to segregate and develop high residual stresses when processed with full melting techniques.
generation.intervention: Adopt a non-melting, binder jetting or 3D ink‐extrusion process to form a green body, then consolidate via isothermal sintering.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled atmospheres (inert or reducing) with sintering temperatures below the melting point to promote full inter-particle diffusion without full melting; using powder feedstock sizes and distributions typical for mechanically alloyed AlCrFeNiSi.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniformly inter-diffused, fine-grained microstructure with minimal compositional gradients arising from the avoidance of rapid melt-solidification.
generation.mechanism: By eliminating the high thermal gradients inherent in melting-based processes, the binder jetting/ink-extrusion route with isothermal sintering mitigates rapid solidification issues. This allows particles to coalesce slowly, preventing segregation, reducing residual stresses, and consequently lowering defect formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally fabricated LPBF samples, the sintered samples will exhibit a more homogeneous microstructure, lower residual stress levels, fewer hot cracks/pores, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength and ductility).
generation.baseline: Samples manufactured by conventional laser powder bed fusion processes that undergo full melting, typically showing compositional segregation, high residual stress, and defect-related mechanical impairments.
generation.boundary: The expected benefits should be evident for AlCrFeNiSi alloys produced from mechanically alloyed powders under controlled binder jetting and sintering conditions. The effectiveness may vary with powder morphology, sintering profiles, and when scaled beyond laboratory-sized builds.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of mechanical improvement and the precise optimization window for sintering parameters remain uncertain until detailed process-property relationships are established for this specific alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples: one using conventional LPBF and the other using a binder jetting/ink-extrusion process followed by isothermal sintering. Ensure both sets use identical powder feedstock and environmental conditions. After fabrication, subject both sets to identical mechanical and microstructural evaluations.
measurements: Residual stress measurements (e.g., via XRD or neutron diffraction)
Microstructural characterization (via EBSD and TEM to assess grain size and compositional uniformity)
Mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility, and hardness tests)
Defect analysis (quantification of hot cracks, porosity, and segregation via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the binder jetting/sintered samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stress, improved microstructural homogeneity, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the LPBF samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Apart from the currently dominating laser- and electron-beam based AM methods, alternative methods to metal AM have been developed, such as binder jetting and 3D ink-extrusion printing where first a binder-containing green body is shaped at ambient temperature from elemental or pre-alloyed powders that is then densified in a subsequent isothermal sintering step. These techniques have the potential to provide segregation-free, structurally-homogeneous alloys with low residual stress due to full inter-diffusion and isothermal sintering, while also reducing cost and eliminating the need of inert-gas processing environments of beam-based AM. The inks for 3D ink-extrusion can be produced from alloyed metal powder, elemental powder or compounds that reduce (e.g., oxides) or decompose (e.g., hydrides) to metal upon thermal processing. The elimination of pre-alloying steps (i.e., to create powders for selective laser melting) and the ability to directly produce alloys from blended pure oxide feedstock further reduce cost, time, and provide full flexibility of alloy composition. High entropy alloys (HEAs) and their closely related variants, called multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), are the topic of a rather new area of research, and so far, the gathered knowledge is incomplete. This is especially true when it comes to material libraries, as the fabrication of HEA and MPEA samples with a wide variation in chemical compositions is challenging in itself. Additive manufacturing technologies are, to date, seen as possibly the best option to quickly fabricate HEA and MPEA samples, offering both the melting metallurgical and solid-state sintering approach. Within this study, CrFeNiTi MPEA samples were fabricated via laser powder-bed fusion (PBF-LB) and solid-state sintering of mechanically alloyed powder feedstock. The main emphasis is on the PBF-LB process, while solid-state sintering serves as benchmark. Within a volumetric energy density (VED) window of 50 J/mm3 to 83 J/mm3, dense samples with large defect-free sections and an average micro-hardness of 965 HV0.1 were fabricated.
